articles.title: Why we separate collected changes from published releases
articles.description: Field note on keeping ReleaseLog's candidate collection stage apart from the publication application step, and on what our controlled normalizer fixtures do and do not establish.
articles.evidenceScope: Evidence is five controlled normalizer fixture cases recorded 2026-11-10 plus project records of the collection and application code paths. It covers decision validation at the configured threshold only; it does not cover upstream factual accuracy, the application path's other checks, or any live publication.

sections.heading: The problem: a collected candidate is not a release
paragraphs: In our release-feed pipeline, collection creates candidates. Review then proposes a decision with a supplied confidence score, and a separate application step handles publication. These are distinct states. Finding a changed page is useful evidence to inspect, but it does not by itself establish a release that belongs on the public timeline. The normalizer sits between the review output and the application path, checking whether the proposed decisions form an acceptable response for the supplied candidate set.

The application path has further checks beyond this decision validation. It looks up the pending candidate and enqueues release notifications when publication happens. That makes its side effects different from a function that normalizes JSON. Our controlled checks did not invoke publication or send notifications. These notes concern the release-feed path; the editorial guides are separately reviewed, versioned content and do not become articles through candidate approval.

sections.heading: What the controlled fixtures recorded
paragraphs: On 2026-11-10 we ran controlled fixtures for the decision normalizer: five cases, executed without calling any model, database or external service. At the configured threshold the normalizer approved a 0.85 score and converted a 0.84 score to rejection. Missing, unknown and duplicate candidate decisions were rejected by validation as invalid decision sets. The recorded limit deserves repeating in spirit: this tests the normalizer only, and no release was published during the check.

sections.heading: Why the boundary earns its keep
paragraphs: The separation matters because the two stages fail in different ways. Collection can find overlapping material, and review output can omit a decision, name an unknown candidate, or repeat a candidate ID. Those are distinct problems: duplicate decision IDs concern the review response; duplicate announcements concern the content itself. Publication is where notifications go out and public state changes. Keeping a validation-only normalizer in front of a side-effecting application path provides an explicit point at which malformed decision sets can be rejected before application.

The 0.85 figure is a configuration threshold, not an accuracy probability. Nothing in the fixtures calibrates the score against outcomes, and the normalizer does not verify upstream facts. A candidate at 0.86 is approved for application in the mechanical sense, not 86 percent likely to be true. Respecting that distinction in release notes is part of the same discipline.

sections.heading: What these checks do not tell us
paragraphs: Five fixture cases establish that the normalizer's decision table behaved as configured on the run date. They do not establish that every future candidate will be well-formed, that the application path's other checks are correct, or that upstream collection is factually accurate. The normalizer tests verify no upstream facts and publish no releases; those remain separate concerns with separate evidence.

sections.heading: Checklist: keeping the two stages apart
items: Label collection output as candidates in every artifact, log line and draft document.
Reject incomplete decision sets, unknown candidate IDs and repeated candidate decisions; do not let a high score excuse invalid structure.
Record the confidence cutoff as a configured threshold in run notes; never describe it as accuracy or truth probability.
When testing publication, use isolated resources and stub notification delivery to check which actions enqueue it; the five normalizer cases here do not test that behaviour.
Keep normalizer checks free of real credentials and public side effects; test the application path separately with isolated fixtures.

articles.title: Event dates and stable identity: lessons from our reset feed
articles.description: Field note on how our reset feed parser canonicalizes post URLs, rejects future dates and forecast status, and merges duplicate records while preserving the published slug.
articles.evidenceScope: Evidence is six synthetic parser fixture cases recorded 2026-11-10 plus the reset parser project record. It covers URL canonicalization, date and status rejection, and duplicate merge behavior on supplied fixtures only; it does not cover other release sources, false-positive rates, or whether real announcements occurred.

sections.heading: The problem: one announcement, many URLs, one identity
paragraphs: A reset feed has two jobs that pull against each other. It must normalize the many shapes a post URL can take, and it must keep a stable identity for an announcement that has already been published once. The parser project record describes the intended behavior: supported post URLs are canonicalized, tracking-query variants are ignored, and future dates and forecast status are rejected in the supplied fixtures. Without canonicalization the same announcement can appear several times; without identity preservation, re-ingesting an already-published announcement can silently change its public slug.

The record also carries a caution we treat as part of the design: accepting a URL shape or an allowlisted handle is not proof that an actual announcement happened. The parser gates structure, not events.

sections.heading: What the controlled fixtures recorded
paragraphs: The 2026-11-10 controlled run covered six parser cases on synthetic inputs, with no model, database or external service involved. Tracking-query variants collapsed to one canonical post ID. A future date was rejected, and forecast status was rejected. A fixture announcement dated November 1 was checked against a November 10 reference date and retained its November 1 event date rather than being re-dated. Two copies of the same record merged into one, and the merged record kept the existing published slug, recorded as 'already-published-fixture-slug'.

sections.heading: Why event dates and identity need separate rules
paragraphs: The November 1 fixture is the case most worth writing down. When an old announcement is checked against a much later reference date, the temptation is to treat the check date as the event date. The recorded behavior keeps the original event date, which is what a reader of a reset timeline needs: when something was announced, not when we happened to re-verify it.

Merging duplicates while preserving the published slug is the identity half of the same discipline. A slug is a public contract; if re-ingestion generated a new one, existing links would break for no editorial reason. Keeping the already-published slug preserved the reader-facing identity for the duplicate inputs in this fixture.

Merge order matters in this implementation. The helper processes the supplied lists in order and retains the first identity it sees, so supplying the existing published records before incoming records preserves the old slug in our fixture. That is a caller responsibility worth checking. A canonical post ID handles tracking variants; it does not decide which of two conflicting descriptions is more trustworthy.

sections.heading: Limits of parser fixtures
paragraphs: These are synthetic parser inputs. Six passing cases say the canonicalization, date and merge rules behaved as specified on the run date; they do not say every release source has clean dates, that deduplication is universal, or that false positives are impossible. And because the parser only accepts structure, none of this is independent evidence that a real announcement occurred. Structure checks and event verification remain separate gates.

sections.heading: Checklist: dates and identity in a reset feed
items: Canonicalize supported post URLs and ignore tracking-query variants before any deduplication step.
Reject future-dated entries and forecast-status entries at parse time. If rejection reasons are needed operationally, capture them outside a parser that returns null.
Preserve the original event date when re-checking old announcements against a later reference date.
On merge, retain the existing published slug rather than generating a new identity.
Record parser checks as structure validation; never present them as confirmation that an event happened.

articles.title: Why our page check counted six markers but only three cards
articles.description: Field note on a raw-marker counting error in a prior release check, the handoff timing mistake recorded alongside it, its correction, and what our bounded same-day observations do and do not prove.
articles.evidenceScope: A controlled fixture and a pre-batch public HTML snapshot each contain six raw markers and three parsed article nodes. The linked prior-release record separately describes 20 later candidate checks and five handoff probes. These are bounded observations, and DOMParser does not execute or hydrate scripts.

sections.heading: The problem: a counting assertion that measured the wrong thing
paragraphs: Our prior public release carried a page-level acceptance check that counted raw occurrences of a data attribute marker in served HTML. The recorded acceptance note describes what went wrong: Next's serialized data duplicated a data attribute name, so the served page contained six raw marker occurrences for what parsed to three actual guide cards. The old assertion, keyed to the raw count, failed although three cards existed. A check that counts markers in serialized HTML is not counting rendered articles; it is counting string occurrences, and serialization can inflate them.

sections.heading: The recorded handoff timing mistake and its correction
paragraphs: The same record describes a second, more serious defect, and we state it plainly rather than smoothing it over: the outer switch shell lacked failure propagation and began handoff before the complete candidate HTTP gate had finished. The gate did not work before handoff in that release; a still-running gate was overtaken. Afterward the switch script was changed to require candidate, browser and image-provenance acceptance receipts, to make successful gate completion a prerequisite in that switch path.

sections.heading: What the controlled checks and snapshots recorded
paragraphs: The controlled fixture contains six raw marker occurrences and three parsed article nodes. A separate public snapshot of the guides page collected at 09:06 UTC on November 10, before this batch, shows the same counts. This is a historical three-card snapshot, not an assertion about the number of articles on the site today. The prior-release acceptance record separately states that all 20 candidate HTTP routes eventually passed, after handoff had already begun, and that five homepage probes observed during that handoff had no failures. The receipt requirement was added afterward. Those observations do not make the original sequencing correct or prove universal zero downtime.

sections.heading: Why parsed nodes beat raw markers
paragraphs: Counting parsed article nodes counts discrete card elements in the HTML document rather than repetitions inside serialized data. Counting raw marker occurrences measures serialization artifacts, which is why the numbers diverged. The useful change is to measure document elements. Visibility and interaction still need browser checks. We also keep in mind the recorded limit of the fixture method: DOMParser does not hydrate or execute scripts, so the parsed-node count verifies structure, not interactive behavior. Real browser interaction tests remain a separate gate, which is one reason the corrected switch script requires a browser acceptance receipt in addition to the HTTP gate.

There is a second measurement question after counting the cards: which candidate did the acceptance result describe? A browser receipt from an earlier image cannot establish that a later image passed. For this batch, the switch prerequisites are checked against the intended source revision and image. This keeps completion evidence attached to the artifact being considered rather than merely to a familiar filename.

sections.heading: Checklist: acceptance checks that count what matters
items: Count parsed article nodes, not raw attribute-marker occurrences, when asserting rendered card counts.
Expect serialized data to duplicate attribute names; never key pass/fail to raw string counts.
Propagate gate failures to the switch shell, and block handoff until every gate has completed rather than merely started.
Require candidate, browser and image-provenance acceptance receipts before any handoff begins.
Describe handoff probes as observations from that handoff; keep the later gate correction separate from what was actually checked before traffic moved.

articles.title: What our static-asset rollback checks actually prove
articles.description: Field note on the immutable-path merge and byte-comparison checks behind our static asset rollback, the small controlled reproduction we recorded, and the compatibility, provenance and database limits it does not cover.
articles.evidenceScope: Evidence is a three-case controlled reproduction of the immutable-path merge check recorded 2026-11-10 plus the recorded acceptance note for the prior UI release. It covers path merge, old-hash preservation and byte-mismatch rejection only; it does not cover all browser sessions, Docker provenance or database rollback safety.

sections.heading: The problem: rolling forward content while old tabs keep loading
paragraphs: A static-asset rollback strategy lives or dies on path immutability. The recorded behavior of the prior release is that the old public container was retained, old and new immutable static asset paths were merged, and same-name files were compared byte for byte before the merge was accepted. The retained container provides a runnable target for traffic rollback. Merging paths keeps the old asset URLs available when an already-open tab requests them, which addresses one compatibility requirement without proving that the whole session will work.

sections.heading: What the controlled reproduction recorded
paragraphs: The 2026-11-10 controlled reproduction is deliberately small: three cases, with no model, database or external service called. It starts with two files, adds one new path, and ends with three merged files. The old content hash is preserved across the merge. When different bytes appear at the same path, the merge is rejected. The recorded limit is explicit: this is a small reproduction of the immutable-path check, not a test of all browser sessions, Docker provenance or database rollback.

sections.heading: Traffic rollback is not database restoration
paragraphs: The clearest lesson in the record is the boundary between two kinds of rollback. Traffic rollback points requests back to the retained old application and needs a healthy old application as well as available assets. Database restoration is a separate operation with separate evidence. For the UI release in question, the record states that no schema or financial or accounting write occurred, so this particular UI change did not require undoing a data migration. A release that writes data needs its own compatibility and recovery assessment; an asset check cannot answer those questions.

The reproduction also does not establish that every browser tab keeps working. It verifies that old paths survive a merge with their bytes intact; it does not exercise real browser sessions, and it says nothing about Docker image provenance. Those remain untested by this check.

sections.heading: Why a matching path needs matching bytes
paragraphs: Keeping both generations of filenames is only useful if each name continues to identify the same bytes. A same-path collision deserves rejection rather than an arbitrary choice of which file wins: either choice could change the response an old page receives at a URL it already knows. The reproduction makes this decision visible with one accepted shared path and one rejected conflicting path.

This is also why the merge and rollback checks need separate receipts. A successful merge answers a question about files; selecting the old application answers a question about traffic. Neither establishes the origin of the Docker image, the health of every route, or database compatibility. Before a real handoff, those questions still need their own acceptance evidence. Retaining the old target buys an option, not proof that invoking it will always succeed.

sections.heading: Checklist: static asset rollback invariants
items: Retain the previous public container until the new release is accepted, so traffic rollback stays available.
Merge old and new immutable asset paths, then check both generations of URLs; URL availability alone does not verify every old browser session.
Compare bytes for any same-name path before accepting the merge, and reject the merge on any difference.
Record schema and data changes separately. Assess backward compatibility and recovery before choosing a traffic rollback or any database restoration.
Verify the old application is healthy before directing traffic back; keep image provenance and route checks separate from the file-merge result.

articles.title: Claude Prompt Caching: Diagnosing Misses and Designing Stable Prefixes
articles.description: A source-backed guide to reading Claude prompt caching usage fields, diagnosing cache misses, and arranging tools, system prompts and messages into a stable ordered prefix.

sections.heading: What prompt caching reuses
paragraphs: Claude prompt caching reuses an identical input prefix; it is not an answer cache. The documented hierarchy is tools, then system instructions, then messages. Cache lifetime options are five minutes and one hour, subject to the selected model and platform. Exact-prefix matching and model-specific minimum lengths matter.

The usage fields distinguish cache reads, new cache writes and uncached input. Their sum is total input; generated output is separate. A small input_tokens value alone therefore does not describe the complete input ledger.

Tool-definition changes invalidate their prefix and later content. Changing tool_choice affects message caching, not the earlier tool and system caches. An already cache-enabled server-tool loop can receive automatic breakpoints on tool results.

sections.heading: A useful first hypothesis: unstable inputs
paragraphs: Treat a low hit rate as a diagnosis problem, not a verdict on the feature. Begin with a small repeatable workflow and ask what is allowed to change between requests. A request timestamp in shared instructions and a dynamically assembled tool catalog deserve different fixes; changing everything together makes the cause harder to identify.

In a hypothetical support assistant, a randomized greeting is inserted before otherwise shared policy text. The owner wants current answers, but the greeting adds no policy value. Our recommendation is to remove that decorative variation from shared instructions, while retaining the actual policy revision. Do not freeze a changing policy merely to obtain more hits.

sections.heading: A bounded diagnostic walkthrough
paragraphs: This walkthrough is hypothetical, not a measured deployment. First choose a small fixed set of repeat requests and record all three input counters. Confirm that the model supports the intended cache controls and that the shared prefix meets its minimum length. This avoids debugging prompt order when the request is not eligible in the first place.

Next, compare two complete request objects. Keep a separate list of request-level settings such as tool_choice; they cannot simply be moved into a later text paragraph. For content differences, locate the first changed segment and decide whether it is essential. Make one change, replay the same sample, and inspect the counters again.

Stop reordering once the remaining variation is required by the task and eligible repeats behave consistently. Investigate lifetime, workload frequency or platform behavior separately. This stopping rule prevents an open-ended exercise in optimizing a counter while silently changing what the assistant is asked to do.

sections.heading: Checklist: keeping a prefix cacheable
items: Map shared content in the documented tools → system → messages hierarchy.
Record the model, platform, cache controls and minimum cacheable length for the test.
Keep request-level settings comparable while diagnosing a specific content change.
Move volatile text after the last reusable breakpoint only when the intended instructions remain equivalent.
Update changed policies and retrieved evidence even when that produces an expected miss.
Compare cache reads, writes and uncached input together; use the interactive ledger below.
Stop when remaining changes are necessary, and record which hypothesis you will investigate next.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs to accept knowingly
paragraphs: Freshness and reuse are separate design decisions. A cache lifetime is not permission to keep an obsolete document in your prompt. If the upstream document changes, update the supplied content; exact matching then determines reuse. Any application that continues sending an old document has an application freshness problem, not a cache that independently chose stale instructions.

A successful counter also does not settle the business case. Compare complete usage and the current platform bill against a suitable baseline before declaring savings. For mostly unique requests, repeated prompt rearrangement may add maintenance without producing useful reuse. Preserve a short test record so the next engineer can see why the layout exists.

articles.title: Claude Code Hooks: What Blocks Before Versus What Runs After
articles.description: A practical guide to placing Claude Code command-hook checks before actions and automation after them, with explicit limits for async work and security boundaries.

sections.heading: Two phases, different powers
paragraphs: This guide focuses on command hooks: external programs attached to Claude Code lifecycle events. The documentation also supports prompt- and agent-based hook types, so the word hook alone does not imply deterministic execution.

For a synchronous PreToolUse command hook, exit code 2 can prevent the proposed tool call. PostToolUse occurs after the call, so it cannot prevent the original action. Event-specific output rules matter. Async command hooks do not hold up the action and cannot retroactively block it.
These mechanisms support checks, formatting and notifications. Hook files themselves are executable configuration, and the official guide shows why they need deliberate placement and review.

sections.heading: The failure scenario: gating in the wrong phase
paragraphs: Imagine a team that wants edits to generated files rejected. A check that runs only after a write can report the violation, and might attempt a repair, but the original mutation has already happened. Reversal and prevention are different requirements. Decide which one the workflow actually needs before selecting an event.

The opposite mistake is to put every slow task in the pre-action path. A formatting pass does not need veto power just because it belongs in the workflow. Our design rule is to separate fast admission decisions from work that observes or transforms the accepted result, then give each one an explicit completion condition.

sections.heading: A hypothetical CI workflow
paragraphs: Consider a hypothetical repository with an authored source directory and a generated output directory. No deployment or benchmark is implied by this example.

A short synchronous pre-action check rejects direct file-editing tool calls to the generated directory. The team separately uses a post-edit formatter for the files it owns. That formatter finishes before those same files are edited again; putting a mutating formatter in the background would create a race with later edits.

Read-only reporting or a notification can run asynchronously where appropriate. A required CI check still gates a merge or release: an agent finishing its task does not establish that background tests passed. Script and configuration changes receive review because they change how the workflow behaves.

This hook arrangement covers the named tool events only. It does not confine shell processes or replace repository permissions, isolated execution and protected release controls. Keep those boundaries outside the model and outside a small command-matching rule.

sections.heading: Checklist: assigning work to the right phase
items: Write the requirement as prevention, repair, verification or notification.
Use a synchronous pre-action decision when a proposed action must not happen.
Check the specific event schema and exit-code behavior for the installed version.
Serialize formatters or other work that mutates files still being edited.
Use background execution only when the task can safely outlive the tool action.
Make required CI results an explicit release condition rather than assuming a background launch succeeded.
Review the hook code and record which event paths it covers; test a permitted case and a blocked case.

sections.heading: Tradeoffs and the sandbox line
paragraphs: The stopping point is a small, explainable workflow. Every hook should have one owner, one purpose and a visible outcome. If an operation fails, the operator should know whether the original action was blocked, completed with a failed follow-up, or is still waiting on another gate. A generic success message hides these distinctions.

Command hooks are a good fit for conditions that can be evaluated mechanically. When judgment is needed, the documented model-based hook types or another review process may help, but that choice does not turn their decision into an operating-system security boundary. Keep a short rationale for the mechanism you choose instead of expanding a blocklist indefinitely.

articles.title: vLLM Prefix Caching: Deciding Whether a Workload Fits Reuse
articles.description: A source-backed guide to judging whether a vLLM workload's prefix shape justifies automatic prefix caching, with a hypothetical measurement plan and tenant salt tradeoffs.

sections.heading: What the feature does — and does not promise
paragraphs: vLLM automatic prefix caching reuses matching input computation, including in shared-document and multi-turn workloads. Its feature guide distinguishes this prefill work from generating new output tokens; a long generated answer can still dominate end-to-end time. Check the installed release and architecture rather than assuming a default configuration.

The design uses hashed cache blocks and describes eviction when blocks are reused. An optional per-request cache_salt partitions prefix reuse. This is not a fixed five-minute or one-hour API cache contract, and cache matching is not application authorization.

sections.heading: Workload fit is a shape question
paragraphs: Our first question is whether requests have a reusable leading sequence, not whether the feature sounds inexpensive. A document shared across many questions is a different cohort from personalized prompts that diverge near the beginning. Test these cohorts separately so that a large group of unique requests does not hide useful reuse elsewhere.

In a hypothetical service, every tenant has a different long preamble and only occasional requests. Turning on caching alone does not create repetition. Before changing prompt structure, ask whether the text represents a real access or behavior requirement. Combining private contexts merely to increase reuse would solve the wrong problem.

Also distinguish a prompt-processing opportunity from the user-visible objective. A cohort can have substantial repeated input while its long answers still take most of the response time. Decide in advance whether you care about time to first token, total latency or throughput, rather than treating those measurements as interchangeable.

sections.heading: A hypothetical measurement plan
paragraphs: The following plan is hypothetical; it is not a report of measured gains. Classify a representative sample into shared-document, conversational and unique-preamble traffic. Keep only authorized requests in each experiment, and record the configuration and output limits.

For a promising cohort, compare cache-enabled and cache-disabled runs under otherwise comparable conditions. Include cold and warm periods and enough cache pressure to resemble the intended workload. Look at the latency distribution and error rate as well as throughput; one attractive average is not sufficient evidence for adoption.

Choose the target metric and acceptable regression bounds before running the comparison. Stop when repeat runs support a clear decision under those bounds. If the result changes with traffic composition, document separate cohort decisions or postpone adoption. Do not turn an inconclusive experiment into a universal speedup claim.

sections.heading: Checklist: a bounded fit assessment
items: Record the exact serving version, model architecture and cache setting used in the test.
Separate request cohorts by actual leading-token similarity and authorization scope.
Include cache pressure and eviction in the plan instead of assuming a fixed TTL.
Keep concurrency, sampling and output limits comparable across the on/off runs.
Report the selected latency or throughput metric alongside errors and regression bounds.
Write down the decision and the traffic change that would justify repeating the experiment.

sections.heading: Tenant partitioning: the salt tradeoff
paragraphs: The salt mechanism gives an application a way to partition reuse. Our recommendation is to assign the intended cache scope at a trusted application boundary after authenticating the request, instead of accepting arbitrary tenant-supplied scope labels as evidence of entitlement.

That choice has a practical tradeoff: separate tenant scopes can forfeit reuse of otherwise identical material. Treat the loss as part of the isolation design rather than as a cache bug. Do not relax the boundary simply to improve a hit counter.

A cache salt is not a substitute for authorization, a dedicated security boundary or a complete privacy review. Enforce access policy before reaching the model server and treat cache reuse as an additional behavior to verify. The source documents establish the mechanism; this placement advice is our operational analysis.
